label: Metrizing Abstract Simplicial Complexes
notes: This appendix to section I.7 occupies printed pages 123 through 130 and answers a single practical question: given only combinatorial incidence data, how do we manufacture an honest length metric? We preview the recipe of realizing each abstract simplex as a model simplex and gluing along faces.

label: Abstract Simplicial Complexes
notes: We recall the purely combinatorial datum: a vertex set and a family of finite subsets closed under taking subsets. Nothing metric is present yet, only incidence. The emphasis is that this is bookkeeping about which vertices span a face, deliberately stripped of any geometry.

label: The Model Simplex
notes: Each abstract n-simplex is realized by one model simplex from constant curvature geometry. The standard choice is the regular Euclidean simplex with unit edge lengths, but the construction allows any prescribed edge lengths satisfying the simplex inequalities. This model carries the local metric.

label: Edge-Length Assignment
notes: The metric data is an assignment of a positive length to each edge. For the simplex to be realizable in a constant curvature model space the edge lengths must satisfy the simplex inequalities; the regular unit-edge choice always works. This is where geometry first enters the combinatorics.

label: Gluing by Face Identifications
notes: We assemble the realization as a disjoint union of model simplices, one per abstract simplex, quotiented by the face identifications dictated by incidence. Compatibility requires that whenever two simplices share an abstract face the corresponding model faces are glued by an isometry respecting edge lengths.

label: The Intrinsic Length Metric
notes: Distance between two points is the infimum of lengths of piecewise paths crossing finitely many simplices. Each path segment is measured inside one model simplex; the total is summed. This induced or quotient length metric is the canonical metric on the realization, built from the local pieces.

label: The Geometric Realization
notes: The resulting space is the geometric realization carrying its standard piecewise-Euclidean, or more generally piecewise constant curvature, metric. Each open simplex isometrically embeds its model interior; the global object is an M-kappa simplicial complex. We now ask when this length space is well behaved.

label: When Is It a Length Space?
notes: A subtlety: the infimum defining distance might fail to be achieved, or two points might be joined by no rectifiable path of finite length. The shapes condition controls this. With finitely many isometry types of simplices the local geometry is uniformly bounded, ruling out degeneracy.

label: Completeness and Geodesics
notes: Bridson and Haefliger's theorem states that if the realization has only finitely many isometry types of simplices, then the induced length metric is complete and the space is a geodesic space. Local finiteness gives local compactness; the finite shapes bound supplies the uniform control needed.

label: Metric vs Weak Topology
notes: Two natural topologies compete: the metric topology from the length metric and the weak topology, in which a set is closed exactly when its intersection with every closed simplex is closed. They coincide precisely when the complex is locally finite; otherwise the weak topology is strictly finer.

label: Recap and Takeaways
notes: We recap the pipeline: combinatorial complex, model simplices with prescribed edge lengths, gluing by face isometries, intrinsic length metric. The finite shapes condition delivers a complete geodesic M-kappa complex, and local finiteness reconciles the metric and weak topologies. This metrization underpins the whole non-positive curvature program.
